Two contrasting tropical convection
modes from the eastern Paciﬁc to
northern Africa that drive Eurasian
teleconnections in boreal summer
Check for updates
Zhiwei Zhu1,2
, Liaoyuan Shao1,2, Rui Lu1,2 & Wenjian Hua1,2
Eurasian teleconnections in boreal summer signiﬁcantly inﬂuence regional climates and extremes, yet
their dynamic origins remain largely unclear. Here, we revealed two critical modes of tropical
convection that drive these Eurasian teleconnections in boreal summer. The ﬁrst mode is
characterized by suppressed convection in the equatorial eastern Paciﬁc, coupled with enhanced
convection extending from the equatorial Atlantic to northern Africa. In contrast, the second mode
displays similar suppressed convection in the equatorial eastern Paciﬁc, but features enhanced
convection in the Gulf of Mexico and the equatorial Atlantic. These two modes result in markedly
different atmospheric teleconnections, leading to distinct surface air temperature anomalies across
the Eurasian continent. Both modes arise from the combined effects of sea surface temperature
anomalies in the eastern Paciﬁc and the North Atlantic/Indian Ocean. This study offers new insights
into dynamics and seasonal predictions of boreal summer Eurasian climates.
As the world’s largest landmass, the Eurasian Continent is home to
approximately 70% of the global population and serves as a vital region for
agriculture and livestock production. It is characterized by complex topo-
graphy and distinctive boundary layer features across different regions,
resulting in the region’s high sensitivity to climate change. In the context of
global warming, the Eurasian surface air temperature (SAT) has exhibited
the most pronounced warming trends since the 1950s1–3, corresponding to
the rise in more intense and more frequent extreme climate and weather
events during the boreal summer4.
As internal forcings, Eurasian teleconnections play a more direct and
important role in regional weather/climate and their extremes5–7. For
instance, two Rossby-wave trains with zonal-oriented structures led to
extremeheatwavesinEuropeanRussiaandcatastrophicﬂoodinginPakistan
in summer 20108–10. The Rossby-wave train induced by the Atlantic Ocean
sea surface temperature (SST) dipole resulted in an early northward shift of
the westerly jet, which in turn led to an intense Mei-Yu pattern affecting the
Yangtze River Delta, the Korean Peninsula, and southern Japan in summer
202011,12. The subtropical North Atlantic warming and the sea-ice losses
jointly shaped the Eurasian Rossby-wave train, leading to a northwestward
displacement of the western North Paciﬁc anticyclone and unprecedented
extreme rainfall in central and eastern China in July 202113,14. The down-
stream circulation associated with the North Atlantic Oscillation led to a
prolonged extreme heatwave accompanied by drought conditions in the
middle and lower reaches of the Yangtze River basin in summer 202215,16.
Theseextremeevents,whichresultedinsevereeconomiclossesandfatalities,
are all closely tied to the Eurasian teleconnections. Therefore, investigating
the Eurasian boreal summer teleconnections and underlying formation
mechanisms holds substantial scientiﬁc and practical signiﬁcance.
Thus far, two major atmospheric teleconnection modes over the
Eurasian Continent in the boreal summer have been identiﬁed. The ﬁrst
mode is the Silk Road Pattern (SRP), extracted by the ﬁrst empirical
orthogonal function (EOF) mode of the interannual variability of upper
meridional winds from Northwest Africa to East Asia5,17,18. The primary
active centers of this pattern are located around Europe, the Caspian Sea,
Mongolia, and the Korean Peninsula17,19. Horizontally, the SRP is char-
acterized by quasi-stationary Rossby waves propagating along the sub-
tropical jet stream, while vertically, it exhibits a quasi-barotropic structure
with maximum amplitude near the tropopause19. The positive and negative
phases of the SRP are closely linked to SATs and precipitation anomalies
over Eurasia and the Asian summer monsoon system2,20. Furthermore, the

SRP inﬂuences the intensity and regional distribution of extreme events by
affecting atmospheric circulation anomalies21,22. The SRP is also considered
to be a portion of the circumglobal teleconnection (CGT) pattern23,24 over
Eurasia25–28.
The second mode is the British–Baikal Corridor (BBC) pattern. This
mode represents the ﬁrst EOF mode of the upper meridional wind in the
region with the strongest Rossby-wave activity in northern Eurasia. The
primary activity centers are located in the United Kingdom, the Baltic Sea,
Western Siberia, and Lake Baikal. Its horizontal structure appears as sta-
tionaryRossbywavespropagatingalongthepolarfrontjet,whilethevertical
structure is characterized by a slightly westward-tilted quasi-barotropic
distribution in the middle-to-lower troposphere29. The BBC teleconnection
has a signiﬁcant impact on temperature and precipitation in northern
Eurasia, as well as on the frequency of regional extreme events10,30,31.
These two teleconnection patterns propagating eastward along the
subtropical westerly jet and polar jet32 could be the results of atmospheric
internal variability. Partially induced by Indian summer monsoon heating,
the longitudinal position of the SRP is anchored by barotropic energy
conversion and is maintained through the baroclinic energy conversion
from the jet stream18,33. The BBC teleconnection is primarily activated by
multiscaleinteractionswithintheexitregionoftheNorthAtlanticjetstream
and is self-sustained by gaining available potential energy from the back-
ground mean ﬂow through baroclinic energy conversion29,34,35.
Eurasian
teleconnections
are
also
signiﬁcantly
inﬂuenced
by
ocean–land–atmosphere interactions. In the mid-to-high latitudes, factors
such as North Atlantic SST tripole patterns36, western Russian soil
moisture37, and land surface warming over eastern Europe38 can trigger and
strengthen these teleconnections, thereby resulting in climate impacts. In
the tropics, ﬂuctuations in SSTs over different basins stimulate tropical
convection anomalies, which further result in the formation of Eurasian
teleconnections39–41. The Indian Ocean basin-wide SST warming leads to
local convection, triggering Eurasian teleconnection patterns42,43. Mean-
while, the intensive tropical Paciﬁc positive SST anomalies (SSTAs) induce
more active local convection, leading to teleconnection patterns across
Eurasia propagating along the westerly jet44,45. The tropical Atlantic con-
vection induced by local SSTAs leads to the teleconnection along the Great
Circle route46,47. Apart from the tropical convective activity induced by the
SSTAsoverthethreebasins,diabaticheatinginducedbythetropicalAfrican
monsoon48,49, African biomass burning aerosol50, and photovoltaic solar
farm plating in the Sahara Desert51 are all responsible for the formation of
Eurasian teleconnections.
In summary, although substantial research has been devoted to Eur-
asianteleconnections,owingtotheircomplexnature,whetherandhowthey
are coupledwith tropical forcings remains elusive. While tropical SSTAs are
among the most reliable and signiﬁcant predictability sources of climate
prediction, SSTAs-induced tropical convection anomalies could be direct
drivers of extratropical teleconnections. Therefore, identifying the coupled
modes between the tropical convection and the Eurasian teleconnections
during summer is essential to establish the linkage between tropical SSTAs
and Eurasian teleconnections, which will help to better understand and
predict Eurasian summer climates. Motivated by the potential applications
in seasonal climate prediction, this article aims to address the following two
questions: First, how do the Eurasian teleconnections in boreal summer
couplewiththetropicalconvections?Second,whataretheoceanicoriginsof
the tropical convections that drive these Eurasian teleconnections?

Two critical tropical convection modes
To extract the leading modes of tropical convection from the eastern Paciﬁc
to Africa, an EOF analysis is performed on the OLR over the domain of
10°S–25°N and 140°W–40°E during JJA. This reveals that the ﬁrst EOF
mode exhibits negative convection anomalies in the eastern Paciﬁc and
positive convection anomalies extending from the tropical Atlantic to
northern Africa (Fig. 2a). This distribution is consistent with the ﬁrst MCA
mode between tropical convection and the Eurasian teleconnection
(Fig. 1b). The principal component (PC) of this EOF mode (PC1) is highly
correlated with the temporal expansion coefﬁcient of OLR in the ﬁrst MCA
mode with a correlation coefﬁcient of 0.92 (p < 0.01) (Fig. 2b). Since this
convection mode exhibits negative convection over the eastern Paciﬁc and
positive convection anomalies over the tropical Atlantic to northern Africa,
it is designated as a tropical Paciﬁc to Africa convection dipole mode
(TPAF). The second EOF mode of OLR over the tropical eastern Paciﬁc to
Africa region exhibits negative convection anomalies in the eastern Paciﬁc
and positiveconvectionanomaliesfromtheGulfofMexicototheequatorial
Atlantic (Fig. 2c), which is consistent with the tropical OLR anomalies
pattern in the second MCA mode (Fig. 1e). The PC2 is also consistent with
the temporal expansioncoefﬁcient of OLR in the second MCA mode,with a
correlation coefﬁcient of 0.71 (p < 0.01) (Fig. 2d). Because this mode
represents negative convection over the tropical eastern Paciﬁc and positive
convection anomalies extending from the Gulf of Mexico to the equatorial
Atlantic, it is referred to as a tropical Paciﬁc to Atlantic convection dipole
mode (TPAT).
The dynamic and thermodynamic ﬁelds regressed onto the PC of the
TPAF mode clearly reveal the ﬁrst coupled mode of the Eurasian tele-

anomalies associated with the TPAT mode (Exp_TPAT), a Gill-type
response in terms of the upper-level anticyclonic (lower-level cyclonic)

steady state of the atmospheric response (day 20–25 integration in Fig. 4b)

To further investigate the individual roles of positive and negative
convections in the two modes, we conducted three additional experiments
with separately prescribed heating. The results indicate that the two Eur-
asian teleconnections cannot be full stimulated in the absence of either
negative heating overeastern Paciﬁc orpositive heating over Atlantic/Africa
(Supplementary Fig. S3), suggesting that the Eurasian teleconnections result
from the combined effects of convection anomalies spanning from the
tropical eastern Paciﬁc to northern Africa.
In
summary,
the
large
disparity
between
the
two
tropical
convection–coupled Eurasian teleconnections is rooted in the different
position of the positive convection anomalies from the eastern Paciﬁc to
northern Africa. The displacement of the positive convection anomaly leads
to displacement of the Rossby-wave source, which consequently results in
distinct downstream Eurasian teleconnections. The remaining scientiﬁc
questions arise as to why the two distinct convective modes correspond to a
similar convective anomalies pattern over the Indo-Paciﬁc region. What are
the oceanic origins underlying these two critical tropical convection modes?
In the following section, we intend to reveal the underlying physical
mechanisms.
Oceanic origins of the convection modes
To investigate the oceanic origins, the SST and tropical low-level divergent
wind ﬁelds are regressed onto each PC of the two convection modes.
Associated with the TPAF mode (Fig. 5a), a negative SSTA appears in the
eastern Paciﬁc, as well as an Atlantic Niño-like positive SSTA in the eastern
Atlantic. Additionally, substantial positive SSTAs are observed across the
North Atlantic, similar to the SSTA distribution of the positive phase of the
AMO53. There are no signiﬁcant SSTAs related to this TPAF mode in the
Indian Ocean. In this conﬁguration of the SST gradient between the eastern
Paciﬁc and the Atlantic, there is lower-level divergence and suppressed
convection over the eastern Paciﬁc. The Kelvin-wave response to the Paciﬁc
suppressed convection manifests as westerly anomalies (Fig. 3c), which
transports water vapor (or advects high humidity) to tropical North Africa,
resulting in positive moist enthalpy (Supplementary Fig. S4a, b) and pre-
cipitation anomalies in the African region and thereby forming the TPAF
convection mode. Furthermore, the North Atlantic SSTAs may also con-
tribute to the formation of this TPAF mode. On the one hand, the warm
North Atlantic SSTAs provide sufﬁcient local low-level moisture, ensuring
enough water vapor is transported to North Africa by the westerly wind

(NAT) SST index (see Method) are employed to represent these two SST

An EEP index and IOD index (see Method) are further employed to
reconstruct the PC of the TPAT mode (PC2). While both EEP and IOD
indices are highly correlated with PC2, with signiﬁcant respective correla-

reconstructed PC2_Rec exhibits similar spatial characteristics with those
associated with PC2 (Fig. 5d, f). Therefore, we conclude that the TPAT
convection mode is jointly driven by the EEP SSTAs and the IOD-like
SSTAs over the Indian Ocean.

Discussion
The present study identiﬁes two critical modes of tropical convection
extending from the eastern Paciﬁc to Africa during the boreal summer,
which drive Eurasian teleconnections with distinct climate impacts. The
inﬂuencing mechanisms of these convection modes on Eurasian tele-
connectionsaredemonstrated,andtheoceanicoriginsunderlyingthesetwo
convection modes are investigated.
The EEP SSTs and the NAT SSTs are responsible for the formation of
the ﬁrst convection mode of the TPAF (Fig. 6a). The negative convective
anomalies associated with the cold eastern Paciﬁc SSTAs excite a Gill-type
Kelvin-wave response in terms of westerly anomalies from the equatorial
Atlantic to northern Africa, transporting moisture and enhancing convec-
tion in the region. Meanwhile, the eastern Paciﬁc cold SSTAs together with
the NAT SSTAs intensify the SSTA gradient, resulting in an anomalous
southwesterly ﬂow penetrating inland Africa. The southwesterly ﬂow
transports the water vapor and fosters precipitation and convection over
northern Africa. These ocean–atmospheric processes form the TPAF con-
vective mode, which is characterized by negative convection anomalies in
the eastern Paciﬁc and positive convection anomalies extending from the
tropical Atlantic to northern Africa (left panel of Fig. 6a).
AsaGill-typeRossby-waveresponsetotheTPAF convectionmode,an
upper-level high-pressure (anticyclonic) anomaly is induced over the North
Atlantic. This anticyclonic anomaly acts as a Rossby-wave source, exciting
downstream teleconnections that contribute to non-uniform surface
warmingovertheEurasianContinent(rightpanelofFig.6a).Consequently,
eastern Europe and Northeast Asia are dominated by pronounced positive
SATanomaliesduetothedominantbarotropichigh-pressure(anticyclonic)
anomaly in situ.
The EEP SSTs and the IOD are responsible for the formation of the
second convection mode of the TPAT (Fig. 6b). Similar to the formation of
TPAF, the cold SSTAs in the eastern Paciﬁc still generate local negative
convective anomalies and westerly wind anomalies to their east. However,
owing to the negative IOD-like SSTA, the equatorial westerlies counteract
the easterlies induced by the SST contrast between the Atlantic and western
Indian Ocean. This leads to moisture convergence only in the Gulf of
Mexicoand the equatorial Atlantic, forming the second convection mode of
the TPAT, with negative convection anomalies in the eastern Paciﬁc and
positive convection anomalies in the Gulf of Mexico to the Atlantic (left
panel of Fig. 6b).
In response tothis convection mode of the TPAT, an upper-level high-
pressure (anticyclonic) anomaly is induced in the central part of the North
American continent. This upper-level anticyclonic anomaly acts as a
Rossby-wave source and excites a different downstream Eurasian tele-
connection. The barotropic anomalous anticyclones of the Eurasian tele-
connection dominate western Europe and Lake Baikal, leading to
signiﬁcantly regional negative SAT anomalies (right panel of Fig. 6b).
It is worth noting that large fractional covariance of the ﬁrst MCA
mode may be related to the systematic upward trend in geopotential
height caused by either internal variability or external forcing. While the
decadal to interdecadal climate variability across Eurasia is primarily
driven by the internal decadal variability of the climate system (e.g.,
AMO)2,54,55, changes in anthropogenic greenhouse gas concentrations and
aerosolslevelsalso play rolesintheAMO’s inﬂuenceordirectly contribute
to the recent non-uniform warming observed over the Eurasian
continent56,57. Consequently, the ﬁrst MCA mode proposed in this study
can be regarded as a signiﬁcant mode characterized by trends inﬂuenced
by both internal and external forcing. Although the ﬁrst MCA mode
encompasses trend signals from both internal decadal climate variability
and external forcing, our primary focus is the resultant effect of multiple
factors concerning the Eurasian teleconnection, with the goal of

Thetwoidentiﬁed Eurasianteleconnectionsareindeedlinked torecent
climate extremes. For instance, the catastrophic extreme rainfall event of
July 2021 is closely associated with a mid-latitude Eruasian Rossby wave13
thatresemblesthe Eurasianteleconnectionidentiﬁed inthe ﬁrstmode of the
MCA. Similarly, the record-breaking extreme high temperature experi-
enced in the Yangtze River Basin during July and August of 2022 are related
to a stationary Rossby wave train15, akin to the Eurasian teleconnection
observed in the second MCA mode. The two Eurasian teleconnections in
boreal summer revealed in this study appear to play increasingly signiﬁcant
roles in driving these recent summer weather and climate extremes. In the
present study, we did not assess the performance of climate models in
simulating the two convection modes and their corresponding Eurasian
teleconnections. The potential future changes in these convection modes
and associated teleconnections also remain unclear. These topics are of
signiﬁcant interest and importance, warranting further investigation.
Methods
Datasets used
The datasets used in this study include: (1) monthly mean atmospheric
variables, including zonal and meridional winds and geopotential height,
from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset58 with a horizontal resolution of
0.25° × 0.25°; (2) monthly mean SST obtained from the Met Ofﬁce Hadley
Center Sea Ice and SST dataset59 at a 1.0° × 1.0° resolution; (3) Monthly
mean 2-m air temperature data from the Climatic Research Unit gridded
Time Series (CRU TS version 4.06)60, with a resolution of 0.5° × 0.5°; (4)
Monthly precipitation data from the Global Precipitation Climatology
Project (GPCP) (version 2.3)61, with a 2.5° × 2.5° resolution; and (5)
monthly mean outgoing longwave radiation (OLR) data from NOAA62,
witha2.5° × 2.5°resolution.Alldatasetscovertheperiodfrom1979to2021.
Summer denotes the average of June, July, and August (JJA).
Deﬁnition of indices
We employed three indices: (1) the Equatorial Eastern Paciﬁc (EEP) index,
calculated as the areal mean SST within 8°S–8°N and 170°W–80°W
weighted by SST regression coefﬁcients in each grid (pink boxes in
Fig. 5a, d); (2) the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) index, deﬁned as the areal
mean SST across (25°S–15°N, 45°E–93°E) and (25°S–5°S, 93°E–115°E),
similarly weighted by SST regression coefﬁcients in each grid (green box in
Fig.5d);and (3) the North Atlantic SST (NAT) index, representingthe areal
mean SST in the North Atlantic (0°–70°N), sourced from the NOAA
Physical Sciences Laboratory63.

Numerical model
A linear baroclinic model (LBM)65 is utilized to investigate the mechanisms
suggested by observational diagnoses. The dry model with a T21 horizontal
resolution with 20 vertical sigma levels was employed, with the climatolo-
gical mean for June–August during 1981–2010 serving as the reference
baseline. The model is integrated for 25 days to assess the steady response to
the prescribed diabatic heating, enabling a focused analysis of the atmo-
spheric dynamics inﬂuenced by the speciﬁed heating, thereby enhancing
ourunderstandingoftheEurasianteleconnectionscoupledwiththetropical
convections.
Data availability
The datasets are available in a public repository that assigns persistent
identiﬁers to them. The monthly mean geopotential height and zonal and
meridional wind data are openly available from the ERA5 reanalysis dataset
at https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.6860a573. The monthly mean sea surface
temperature data provided by the Hadley Centre Sea Ice and Sea Surface
Temperature dataset are available at https://www.metofﬁce.gov.uk/hadobs/
hadisst/data/download.html. The monthly mean 2-m air temperature data
from CRU TS v4.06 are available at https://crudata.uea.ac.uk/cru/data/hrg/.
The observed monthly precipitation data provided by the Global Pre-
cipitationClimatologyProject(GPCP)areavailableonline(https://psl.noaa.
gov/data/gridded/data.gpcp.html). The Interpolated Outgoing Longwave
Radiation (OLR) data from NOAA are available at https://psl.noaa.gov/
data/gridded/data.olrcdr.interp.html. The NAT index provided by PSL
(NOAA) can be downloaded at https://psl.noaa.gov/data/timeseries/AMO.
Code availability
The data in this study are analyzed with NCAR Command Language (NCL;
http://www.ncl.ucar.edu/). The relevant codes in this work are available,
upon request, from the corresponding author Z.Z.
